title: Separation of Homogeneous and Inhomogeneous Broadening using Two-Dimensional Coherent Spectroscopy
authors: Adam Alfrey, Cole Tait, Joshua R. Hendrickson, Steven T. Cundiff
abstract: Separating the contributions of homogeneous dephasing from inhomogeneous broadening in spectral linewidths is essential for connecting optical spectra to microscopic dissipation and disorder mechanisms. Voigt fits to one-dimensional spectra, such as photoluminescence, yield strongly correlated Gaussian and Lorentzian widths, so that neither width can be determined independently with confidence. We quantitatively show that two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS) reduces this degeneracy by providing orthogonal spectral slices, diagonal and cross-diagonal, with complementary sensitivity to homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening processes. As a demonstration, we measure the exciton resonance in hBN-encapsulated MoSe$_2$ at 8 K. A joint uncertainty-weighted fit maps the full $χ^2(σ,γ)$ landscape to quantify parameter covariance. Compared with linear Voigt analysis, 2DCS yields more compact confidence regions and markedly reduced parameter correlation, enabling reliable separation of the contributions to the excitonic linewidth.
summary: The paper introduces two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS) as an advanced technique to overcome the ambiguity in separating homogeneous dephasing ($\gamma$) from inhomogeneous broadening ($\sigma$) in optical spectra. By analyzing orthogonal spectral slices, 2DCS provides independent constraints that significantly reduce parameter correlation compared to traditional one-dimensional fitting methods. This allows for a more accurate microscopic understanding of excitonic linewidths in semiconductor quantum dots.
main_problem: The primary challenge is separating the contributions of homogeneous dephasing ($\gamma$) from inhomogeneous broadening ($\sigma$) in measured spectral linewidths, as standard linear fits suffer from parameter degeneracy.
main_result: Two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS) provides orthogonal constraints that significantly reduce the covariance between $\sigma$ and $\gamma$, leading to more reliable and distinct estimates for both parameters compared to one-dimensional photoluminescence (PL) analysis.
method: The authors compare parameter estimation using standard 1D Voigt fitting against a joint fit of two orthogonal spectral slices—cross-diagonal ($S_{	ext{cross}}$) and diagonal ($S_{	ext{diag}}$)—obtained via 2DCS.
model_or_system: The study investigates the exciton resonance in hBN-encapsulated $	ext{MoSe}_2$ at low temperature (8 K). The spectral lineshape is modeled as a convolution of Lorentzian (homogeneous) and Gaussian (inhomogeneous) components, forming a Voigt profile.
key_observables: Linewidth components ($\sigma$, $\gamma$), parameter covariance metrics (Pearson correlation coefficient $ho_{\sigma\gamma}$), and confidence region shapes derived from $\chi^2$ profiling.
important_parameters: Exciton resonance energy, temperature (8 K), homogeneous dephasing rate ($\gamma$), inhomogeneous broadening width ($\sigma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes symmetric Voigt lineshapes; the method relies on the assumption that physical parameters $(\sigma, \gamma)$ are shared across both 2DCS slices in the joint fit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the failure of 1D fits (showing highly elongated covariance contours) versus the success of 2DCS analysis, which yields more compact confidence regions and reduced parameter correlation. The comparison quantifies this improvement using covariance metrics.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical necessity of separating $\sigma$ and $\gamma$. It then details the methodology comparing 1D PL fitting to joint 2DCS fitting across orthogonal spectral slices, culminating in a quantitative comparison of parameter uncertainty reduction.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful spectroscopic tool for characterizing open quantum systems by disentangling intrinsic decoherence mechanisms ($\gamma$) from static disorder effects ($\sigma$), which is crucial for understanding solid-state emitters and quantum materials.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. MoSe2 exciton photoluminescence lineshape is best described by a Voigt profile. Normalized 8 K MoSe2 exciton PL spectrum (open circles), excited by a HeNe laser (632.8 nm, 20 μW average power), overlaid with best-fit Gaussian (red dashed), Lorentzian (blue dashed), and Voigt (black solid) models. The Voigt profile captures both the peaked core and the extended wings more accurately than either single-component model, motivating its use as the phenomenological description for the PL spectrum.
